A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Testing Most Influential Sets, with the same authors, framework and applications. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original 1,000-repetition simulations and influence-testing analyses of geography, sparrows and four machine-learning datasets in Section 4 and Appendices A5–A6.

after.justification: v3 retains original application analyses and reports revised simulation results in Section 4 and Appendix A4. These include estimated distribution parameters and influence-test p-values.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 changes the stated distribution-selection rule from v1's max{xi_x,xi_r} to xi as defined by Theorem 1, namely min{xi_x,xi_r}. This corrects a consequential inconsistency within the retained greedy-selection, block-maxima, MLE and hypothesis-testing pipeline.

E1.justification: Both versions use the four Normal/t(5) simulation combinations and the same geography, sparrow, Law School, Adult Income, Boston Housing and Communities & Crime applications. Revised simulation sample sizes do not introduce different data or task coverage.

E2.justification: No evaluated comparison algorithm is added or removed. Comparisons involving true, uncorrected and bias-corrected Gumbel distributions remain in v1 Figures 1/A3 and v3 Figures 2/A1. Newly cited methods are not evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: The convergence experiment replaces N={100,200,500,1000,2000} with a denser grid spanning 20–1000, emphasizing smaller samples (v3 Figure 3 and Table A1). Application sample sizes, target coefficients and tested subset sizes remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The existing finite-sample sensitivity analysis is extended below N=100, examining departures from asymptotic predictions at much smaller samples. The location/scale estimation diagnostic is retained as v3 Figure A1, formerly Figure A3, and the Communities & Crime subset-cancellation analysis remains in Table A2.

E5.justification: Section 3.3 newly recommends multiple-testing correction when testing several coefficients or subset sizes. No specific correction or application to reported p-values is documented. Simulations retain 1,000 repetitions, means, SDs, quantiles and ±1 SD bands; changed uncertainty values themselves belong to E6.

E6.justification: Table A1 adds smaller-sample results, removes N=2000 and revises shared settings: at N=100, Normal–Normal mean/SD change from 0.0416/0.0319 to 0.0422/0.0788. The Seychelles–Eswatini row changes influence/location/scale from 0.077/0.020/0.004 to 0.091/0.027/0.006, retaining p<1e-16 (v1 Table 2; v3 Table 1). Other application findings remain stable.

T1.justification: Theorem 2 replaces proportional growth k=pN with k→∞ and k/N→0 and revises its CLT argument. Theorem 1 now requires only the heavier tail to be polynomial. Proposition 1 gives an explicit multivariate, optionally penalized formula with a new normal-equations proof, replacing scalar induction and old Appendix A1. The set constraint changes from at most k to exactly k; the perturbation sum and Lemma 2's Gumbel survival expression are also corrected.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contribution: an EVT-based framework for testing excessive influence in linear regression, with efficient exact-influence computation and applications across the same domains. v3 foregrounds the formula and distribution families already central to v1.

C2.justification: Section 5 adds concrete guidance on investigating flagged sets, separate analysis, transparent reporting and avoiding trimming/winsorization. It newly characterizes the test as conservative and expands discussion of selection dependence and delicate EVD estimation. Table A1 also adds an overstated interpretation: its assertion that every theoretical value lies within the reported quartiles is contradicted by several rows.

D1.justification: v1 promises future code availability; v3's Reproducibility Statement supplies a repository link and states that reproduction code is available. This improves access information, although repository contents cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs. Other implementation disclosures remain largely unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds Fisher–Tippett and Gnedenko on EVT, Walker–Birch on ridge influence, and Oorschot–Zhou on estimation. It replaces Nunn (2020) with Nunn–Puga (2012) and removes contextual references including Huber–Ronchetti, Price and Roscher. The overall positioning relative to influential-subset research remains stable; several other bibliography changes merely update publication metadata.

P1.justification: The abstract, background, mathematical exposition and discussion receive substantial rewriting and reorganization. v3 inserts an EVT primer, moves the regression setting into Section 2.3, replaces many numbered subsections with paragraph headings, and consolidates appendix material. These changes substantially reshape the narrative beyond the scientific revisions.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figure 1 comparing individual and maximal influence, replaces the main-text shape-estimate table with a redesigned convergence plot using a nonlinear sample-size axis, and removes the old distribution-visualization Figure A1. Tables and appendix displays are reformatted and consolidated. The original methodology and location/scale plots are retained under new numbers.

improvement.justification: The new normal-equations proof and corrected perturbation and tail-selection formulas improve clarity and internal consistency; smaller-sample evidence and a concrete code link improve validation and reproduction information. These gains are tempered by reporting overstatement: v3 Table A1 claims universal agreement within quartiles, although t(5)–Normal at N=1000 has Q75=0.1771, below the predicted 0.2. Theorem 2 changes its growth regime rather than simply strengthening the earlier guarantee.
